text: Cary High School is one of six public high schools in Cary, North Carolina, and is part of the Wake County Public School System. It became the first state-funded public high school in North Carolina in 1907, when the North Carolina legislature approved a statewide public education system, and the school’s board of directors sold it to the Wake County Board of Education for $2,750 on April 3, 1907—its estimated value at the time was over $8,000—half of which was paid by the state. This made Cary High School the first county high school in North Carolina, the first state-funded high school in the state, and the first high school in the state system. The school opened in 1896 as a private boarding school at the head of Academy Street, established to provide a higher course of instruction than local one-room schools, with its first class graduating in May 1897 and Edwin Lee Middleton serving as its first principal. In 1907, the State Legislature authorized a Cary School District and approved a school tax of up to 30¢ for every $100 of real estate, which was approved by voters in a referendum on May 7, 1907, with 100 in favor and two against. Students from outside the district paid $14 per term for freshmen and sophomores and $16 for juniors and seniors. Middleton remained principal during the transition, retiring in 1908, and was succeeded by superintendent Marcus Baxter Dry. The curriculum included one year of French, three years of science, and four years of English, history, Latin, and mathematics, with arithmetic, algebra, and geometry included in the latter; domestic science was added in 1910 for female students, and students could add art, elocution, music, or piano for an extra fee. In 1912, 119 students enrolled, including eighty boarding students from other counties, and the curriculum expanded to include agriculture, botany, and chemistry. That year, the Girls Athletic Club was formed. By 1913, the student body had outgrown the campus, prompting Dry to request a tax increase for a new building; voters approved $25,000 in bonds for a 33-room brick building, with an additional $5,000 from the state, which was considered the best high school building in the state. Dry noted that many school officials from across the state visited to study it. In 1914, the school changed its name to Cary Public High School and Farm Life School to reflect its expanded vocational curriculum, including agriculture and home economics. The next year, fifteen acres on what is now Walnut Street were donated by James M. Templeton Jr., and an additional $1,500 from others and the Town of Cary funded a barn, farmhouse, dairy cows, and other stock for the model farm (the farmhouse survives at 510 Walnut Street); students in the agricultural program milked the cows and consumed the milk with breakfast. In 1915, the Chsite yearbook premiered; in 1919, students formed a student council, a general athletic association, and The Echo campus newspaper; in 1921, a marching band was formed, school colors of olive green and white were selected, and the white rose became the school flower, with the motto "service." In 1920, Cary voters approved $45,000 in bonds for a new farm life department building, completed in 1922 as the Walter Hines Page Vocational Education Building. The following year, a State Normal Class for Teachers began at Cary High School, one of four sites in the state and operating for five years. By 1924, students could earn academic, agriculture, home economics, or teacher training diplomas. In 1925, a new gymnasium, the James M. Templeton Physical Education Building, costing $12,000, was added, seating 500 and featuring a wooden basketball court; by 1926, campus athletics included baseball, basketball, football, tennis, and track, and student clubs included the Boys Glee Club, Dramatic Club, Girls Glee Club, Home Economics Club, four literary societies, and the Science Cub. In 1926, the school acquired its first bus, traveling 24 miles a day for 22 students; in 1927, the Wake County Board of Education expanded the Cary School District from the Raleigh City limits to the Durham County line, enabling busing to consolidate schools in Morrisville, Reedy Creek, and Sorrell's Grove. The Board allocated $38,000 for a new building and $12,000 for heating upgrades, and the school had a library with 1,970 volumes. During the Great Depression, property values dropped, reducing school tax income; the Board closed Mount Herman and Ebenezer schools and sent their students to Cary; state funding increased and eventually ended the local school tax in 1933. Budget cuts included no new library books and the cessation of the Chsite yearbook; dormitories were closed, ending the boarding era. Grades 1 through 11 were taught at Cary High School under a consolidated program. WPA funding expanded athletic fields by five acres and enabled the construction of a football stadium with seating for 1,500. The success of the football field project led to a collaborative funding effort for a new central school building, with the Board providing $70,000 and the WPA covering the remaining $62,000 of the $132,000 cost. The dedication stone read: "Cary High School – First State Public High School – Established in North Carolina on April 3, 1907," and the building was completed in 1938, though mostly constructed in 1939. The three-story building included a cafeteria, fire doors, first aid room, intercom system, movie projector, sound-proof typing room, and an auditorium with 834 seats. At the dedication on March 4, 1940, Governor Clyde Hoey called Cary a "beacon of hope and inspiration," and the News and Observer noted Cary High School and its predecessor had led secondary education in Wake County and the state for 75 years. In 1941, Cary had the largest high school in Wake County with 460 students; Dry retired after 34 years as principal, then taught algebra in summer school; Thaddeus N. Frye became the new principal. In 1943, the school year was extended from eight to nine months after Wake County added the 12th grade. In 1956, Cary High School became the first in Wake County to be accredited by the Southern Association of Secondary Schools. In 1958, the Wake County Board of Commissioners purchased forty acres for $30,000 from Luther M. Maynard for a new campus; 150 residents debated the location, with some criticizing its distance from downtown and poor road access. Construction proceeded, and the last graduating class to attend the original campus was the Class of 1960, also the first with over 100 graduates. The original campus became Cary Junior High and Elementary School, then Cary Elementary School, and on August 13, 2011, opened as the Cary Arts Center. The new Cary Senior High School campus opened on September 7, 1960, with principal Samuel Arbes; it opened at full capacity with 573 students (sophomores, juniors, and seniors), including three classroom buildings, a gymnasium, library, auditorium, cafeteria, and shop building, designed by William A. Deitrick and built by J. M. Thompson Construction Company of Raleigh, at a cost of $771,251 plus $38,000 for design fees. By 1962, the school needed ten more classrooms, and expansion allowed freshmen to join in 1963, restoring the school’s name to Cary High School. In 1963, the Wake County Board approved the voluntary transfer of six African-American students from Berry O'Kelly School under the "freedom of choice" policy following the U.S. Supreme Court’s desegregation decision; Cary became the first school in Wake County outside of Raleigh to desegregate, selected because it was rapidly changing and more open to change. White parents sued, but the case was dismissed by the North Carolina Supreme Court. The students—seniors Lucille Evans and Frances Louise White, juniors Gwendolyn Matthews and Brenda Lee Hill, sophomore Ester Lee Mayo, and freshman Phyllis Rose—faced intense opposition upon arrival, with protests lasting ten days and dwindling to fewer than fifty students; Evans and White graduated in 1964; Gregory Crowe became the first African American male student in 1964. In 1967, the Board integrated Cary High School by making the former black high school a 9th-grade junior high for all races and transferring all black sophomores, juniors, and seniors to Cary Senior High School, which then had 764 whites and 112 blacks, or a 12.8% minority rate. By 1972, the school was overcrowded and used two mobile classrooms; in 1973, enrollment exceeded 1,500, requiring eight classroom trailers; a county-wide bond referendum provided $700,000 for expansion, with construction beginning in May 1974 on an eight-classroom building for foreign languages, library expansion, auto mechanics shop, stadium field house, and new lobby and offices. In 1989, a $4.5 million construction project added Building 10, including a new air-conditioned media center, allowing freshmen to return to campus after the mid-1960s. In 1995, the school had about 1,800 students in a space designed for 1,455; in 1996, a $3.44 million bond approved improvements including a new classroom, administrative space, Building A renovations for the performing arts, a career center, and computer labs, expanding capacity to 1,585 students, with work beginning on a new main entrance. In 2004, Clark Nexsen approved plans to renovate and expand campus, including a new auditorium, gymnasium, music classrooms, and a new classroom building; construction was completed by J. M. Thompson of Cary, and the new three-story classroom building opened in August 2008. As part of the project, the existing auditorium, band room, Building E, Building F, and part of Building B were demolished—78,063 square feet were removed, 135,839 added, and 26,831 renovated. In 2012, Clark Nexsen designed a master plan for Phase III, including a dining addition and a 100,000-square-foot classroom, to begin when funding is available. As of the 2021–22 academic year, Cary High School had 2,071 students, with 1,080 male and 991 female; the student population was 44.5% White, 27.5% Hispanic, 17.2% Black, 6% Asian, 4.4% two or more races, and 0.3% American Indian, with a total minority population of 55.5%; 28% of students are economically disadvantaged, with 23% receiving free lunch and 4% reduced lunch. The graduation rate is 87%, and 41.7% of students are ready for college, above the district average of 37.8%. The school has 120 teachers with a student-teacher ratio of 17:1; 97% of teachers have three or more years of experience and are certified. The student–counselor ratio is 299:1, better than the state average of 361:1, and the faculty includes a social worker. In 2019, Nolan Bryant received the Maggie Award for Best High School Principal in Western Wake County, and Jerry Dotson, track and cross country coach, received the Maggie Award for Best High School Coach in Western Wake County. Cary High School includes grades 9 through 12 and operates on a traditional calendar with a block schedule. The school offers Advanced Placement® courses, with 53% of students participating and 38% passing at least one AP® exam; 53% of students take the SAT, with an average score of 1146; 64% of graduates pursue college or vocational training. Students have received the Morehead-Cain Scholarship to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and the John T. Caldwell Scholarship to North Carolina State University. Cary High School serves students in grades 9 through 12 and operates on a traditional calendar with a block schedule. The school offers Advanced Placement® courses, with 53% of students participating and 38% passing at least one AP® Exam. Fifty-three percent of students take the SAT, achieving an average score of 1146, and 64% of graduates pursue college or vocational training. Students have received the Morehead-Cain Scholarship to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and the John T. Caldwell Scholarship to North Carolina State University. The Career & Technical Education Department aims to prepare students for employment, incorporating internships into classroom learning, with educational areas including agriculture, business, finance and marketing, career development, computer science and information technology, family and consumer sciences, health sciences, and trade, technology, engineering and industrial education. Since the fall of 2022, the school has included The Academy of Technology and Advanced Manufacturing, a four-year immersive learning community focused on advanced manufacturing, design, engineering, and technology, which received over $100,000 in investment for electrical, electronic, instrumentation, pneumatic/flow control, and robotic equipment. As of 2024, U.S. News & World Report ranks Cary High School 18th in Wake County, 91st in North Carolina, and 3,446th nationally, while Niche gives it an "A" rating and ranks it #95 among the best public high schools in North Carolina. Juniors and seniors with a 3.6 GPA can apply to join the National Honor Society; the top twenty juniors by GPA serve as Junior Marshalls for senior events, and Honor Graduates receive a reception and Academic Awards Night, with students earning gold, silver, or red tassels and a patch for a GPA of 3.75 or higher. The media center employs two staff members and provides access to online databases and a physical book collection, including student-written book reviews on its website. In 1960, the student council held a design contest for a school seal, with the winning design featuring pine cones, dogwood blossoms, and the Latin phrase "Cognito Vincit" or "Knowledge Conquers." The Cary High School Alma Mater is sung to the tune of "Over the Summer Sea" or "La Donna e mobile" from Rigoletto by Giuseppe Verdi; the tune was discovered in 2021 during a performance by the Cary High Marching Band and Concert Chorus at a football game on October 22, 2021, and the revised lyrics are: "Cary! here’s love to thee / And we will ever be / Filled with true loyalty / And with devotion. / Long we will ever claim / The blessings of thy name, / And may thy spirit reign / From crest to ocean. / Fond hearts entwining, / Cease all repining, / Near us is shining / Cary’s bright smile." A tradition involves the rising senior class painting their year on the water tower across Maynard Road, a practice taken over by the Town of Cary for the Class of 1986, with locals contributing to the cost, and the town continuing the tradition. The Cary High School Band, established in 1921, is a corps-style marching band that has gained local, national, and international acclaim, with current director Christopher R. Foster and support from the Cary Band Boosters; it hosts Cary Band Day annually since 1958. In 1959, the band marched in Charlotte's Shrine Bowl Parade, Raleigh's Christmas Parade, and Wilmington's Azalea Festival Parade under James Johnson; in 1963, it represented North Carolina at a national festival in Sioux City, Iowa under Jack White; in 1965, it marched in Governor Dan K. Moore's inaugural parade under A. J. Moore. In 1972, the band won the Sun-Fun Festival in Myrtle Beach, beating Wilson High from Pennsylvania, and was listed in the top twenty nationally by Ruffles and Flourishes; in January 1973, under Jimmy Burns, it became the first North Carolina band to march in the Tournament of Roses parade, raising $30,000 for the trip, and also competed on the television show Sounds of '73, viewed by twenty to thirty million people; it also marched in parades for Governor James Holshouser and President Richard Nixon, and in the King Orange Bowl Festival parade in Miami on December 31, 1973. In August 1974, the band performed at the Fêtes de Genève in Geneva, Switzerland, a yearly honor limited to one U.S. band; the town celebrated Jimmy Burns Day. In 1975, the band played at the Kentucky Derby; on January 1, 1976, it became the first out-of-state band to march in the Cotton Bowl parade in Dallas; later that year, it won the Pennsylvania Festival of the Colonies parade competition and came in third overall. In 1977, the band returned to the Tournament of Roses; in 1978, it participated in the Festival of States in St. Petersburg, Florida, and under Don Stubblefield, it marched in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, seen by eighty million viewers; in March 1980, it toured Romania as Friendship Ambassadors; in 1982, it performed for President Ronald Reagan at a Raleigh Civic Center campaign event and in the Gimbel's Thanksgiving Day parade in Philadelphia; in 1984, it marched in the Tournament of Roses, becoming the first non-California band to do so three times; in 1987, it placed third at the Citrus Bowl Music Festival; in 1989, it marched in the inaugural parade for Governor James G. Martin and the San Diego Holiday Bowl Music Festival. In 1991, the band won the Citrus Bowl Music Festival parade event; in 1993, it marched in the inaugural parade for Governor James B. Hunt; in 1996 under Tony Robinson, it earned fourteen of fifteen first-place awards at the Gator Bowl in Jacksonville, including the Grand Champions trophy for best in both parade and field show. In 2016, the band marched in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade under Matt Minick. The Ambassadors Club represents Cary High to new transfer students and ninth graders during transition. The IDEA Club promotes student engagement and activism in government and politics, participated in fighting censorship of books related to gender, sexuality, and race in the school library in March 2022, and conducts voter registration drives. In 1996, alumnus Del Richards donated $40,000 to launch a Navy Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps (NJROTC) program, which includes competitive teams in academics, athletics, drill, marksmanship, and physical fitness. Cary High School Performing Arts encompasses the choral group and drama club, typically producing a fall play and a spring choral concert; during the pandemic, live performances were replaced with videos edited by alumnus Michael Shorb and streamed to audiences; the group is supported by the Cary High School Performing Arts Booster Club. The school's yearbook, YRAC, began in 1948, reviving a prior publication discontinued during the Great Depression; in 1987, The Spirit student newspaper won first place at the American Scholastic Press Association Writing Contest under Janice Richardson; other student publications include The Page, founded in 2018 by Stephen Atkinson and Claire Perry. The Speech and Debate team is part of the Tarheel Forensics League and competes statewide; formed around 2010, it finished second in its first year, second at the state championship the next year, and qualified for the National Speech and Debate Tournament; it has competed at the national tournament seven of its first ten years and hosts local tournaments. The school's mascot is the Imp; Albert H. Werner, football and baseball coach starting in 1935, influenced the choice, having played at Duke where the junior varsity teams were called the Blue Imps; the name was initially the White Imp to balance college favorites, incorporating the White Phantoms of UNC Chapel Hill; initially used only by the football team, the name was later adopted for all sports; after the 1971–72 school year, "white" was dropped to avoid racial connotations during desegregation, and the Imp is now green. The current Imp illustration was designed by student Lee Mauney in the 1960s, who later became the school's art teacher and athletic director; in January 2010, Cary premiered a costumed Imp mascot at a basketball game against Apex High School, funded by donations and student efforts from the Ambassador Club, produced by Stagecraft in Cincinnati, Ohio. ESPN named the Cary Imp one of the best nicknames for a football team in 2009, and Sports Illustrated recognized it as the fourth most unique high school nickname in 2010; in 2023, the Cary Imp was voted the best high school mascot in the country in the Sports Illustrated High School Fan National annual competition. Historically, the school's colors were olive green and white; today, they are Kelly green and white. Cary's historic rival was Garner High School, noted as "as intense a rivalry as there was," and as the community grew and students were sent to Apex High School, that rivalry became the biggest. Cary is a member of the North Carolina High School Athletic Association (NCHSAA). Co-ed sports include cheerleading, junior varsity cheerleading, cross country, indoor track, track, and swim and dive; women's sports include varsity and junior varsity basketball, golf, gymnastics, lacrosse, soccer, softball, tennis, volleyball; men's sports include varsity and junior varsity baseball, basketball, football, golf, lacrosse, soccer, tennis, and wrestling. The school's first football team was organized in 1917 under Tal Stafford, a former North Carolina A&M All American, who later disbanded the team due to World War I and the influenza epidemic; it was reorganized in 1923, and in 1935, Albert H. Werner became the football coach. In 1955 under John Ebby, the team went undefeated and won the Class A state championship, with players John Yarborough and Charles Maison, who later became an All-American at Elon College. On September 15, 1961, the new campus football field was dedicated as the Paul W. Cooper Athletic Field; in 1970, the Imps Booster Club pledged $100,000 to expand the field with locker rooms, restrooms, showers, and seating; in 1973, a press box was added, and A. E. Finley donated $15,000 to reduce debt, leading to the renaming of the stadium as Cooper Field at A. E. Finley Stadium; in 1982, the press box was replaced for $29,500. In 1976, under coach Dave Riggs, the football team won the conference title with a 6–1 record, winning the first round of the playoffs before losing to undefeated Richmond County High School, marking its best season until 1995; in the 1995–96 season under Bill Devine, the team was undefeated, won the conference title, allowed only 45 points, won their first playoff game, and set records for most points scored in a season and most interceptions, with the second-longest winning streak in school history. Under coach Jerry Winterton from 1981 to 2010, the wrestling team won 19 state championships (11 state tournament and 8 dual team titles), 21 regional championships, and 28 consecutive conference tournament championships; in 1987, it was ranked 25th nationally by Amateur Wrestling News and featured on ESPN's Scholastic Sports America; in 1988, it reached as high as 11th nationally; in 1990, its consecutive match win streak ended at 188 wins. Including playoffs, the Imps had a record of 621–16 under Winterton from 1981 to 2010; during this time, he coached 44 individual state champions and wrestlers who earned All-American and National Champion honors. Winterton was inducted into the Cary High School Hall of Fame in 1995, the North Carolina Chapter of the National Wrestling Hall of Fame in 2004, the NCHSAA Hall of Fame in 2014, and the National High School Hall of Fame (NFHS) in 2017. In 1994, the first class was inducted into the Cary High School Hall of Fame, which includes individuals who have played, coached, or served in the school's athletic program. The school's geographic coordinates are 35°46′18″N 78°45′57″W or 35.7717°N 78.7659°W. The faculty also includes a social worker.
